Memory · Two ways to remember

Recognition versus recall

Recognition is identifying something familiar when it is presented to you. Recall is bringing an answer to mind from memory. Think of choosing a familiar shape from cards versus drawing the shape you remember.

Is the answer in front of you?

Recognition

“Which of these did I see?” The candidates are present. You judge which one matches something in memory.

Like spotting a familiar book cover on a shelf.

Recall

“What did I see?” You supply the answer from memory instead of selecting it from a presented set.

Like saying the book’s title when its cover and a list of titles are out of sight.

Recall can use cues, too. A question, a place, or a hint can help you retrieve an answer. The distinction is whether you identify a presented candidate or generate the answer yourself. [1] [2]

Try the difference

Use a new shape so the illustration cannot supply the answer. Follow the steps in order; a mental answer is enough.

1. Study a shape name

Crescent

Picture this shape, then close this fold before continuing.

2. Recall the shape

With the study fold closed, say or sketch the shape from memory. Try before opening anything below.

Need a cue?

Think of a thin moon.

If this hint helps you supply the shape, you are using cued recall.

3. Show the recognition choices

Which name did you study? Choose mentally from these cards.

  • Circle
  • Crescent
  • Square
Reveal the answer and comparison

Crescent. During recall, you had to supply the shape. During recognition, the answer appeared among the candidates for you to identify.

The moon hint also supplied a cue. Having a cue does not automatically make a task recognition.

This is a teaching exercise, not a memory test. Once you see the choices or answer, you have another exposure to the shape; repeating the exercise cannot fairly compare the two tasks.

Where the picture stops

Memory does not literally store a perfect shape inside a thought bubble. Fold’s drawing is a metaphor for retrieving information; recall can also produce words or other remembered details.

The candidates change what the task asks you to do. The illustration does not show that one process is always easier, accurate, or separate from the other. Real activities can involve both.

  2. Nielsen Norman Group · Recognition vs. Recall in User Interfaces
